The regexes are kept only as a published audit of the 18 disagreements.

studies.title: What a heatwave does to the partnership, and which knob actually moves it
studies.kind: host-symbiont bioenergetic model under thermal stress
studies.question: Four routes on this page claim to raise thermal tolerance by acting on four different things: the symbiont's thermal optimum, its photoprotective capacity, how much oxidative stress it takes to do damage, and how readily the host expels symbionts under that stress. Are they additive, or does one dominate? And what does each cost when there is no heatwave?
studies.summary: The dynamical core is not invented here: it is a line-by-line port of the published coRal model, checked against the author's own R code to 5e-15 relative error across three environments. That matters because coRal contains NO temperature variable at all -- in the published model bleaching is driven by light -- so the thermal coupling is this page's addition and enters through exactly one parameter. The study's weakness is that single calibration: one parameter was tuned so the unmodified holobiont bleaches inside NOAA's 4-8 degree-heating-week window, which means the model cannot then be used as evidence about that window. A second weakness is numerical and is reported as a failure rather than smoothed over: the step-halving check fails at 9%, because coRal integrates with explicit Euler and a first-crossing readout inherits that slow convergence. The absolute threshold is therefore not converged; the knob ranking, which is what the study claims, is identical at three step sizes.
studies.code: results/coral/code/bleaching_dynamics.py (with coral_deb.py and coral_reference_run.R beside it)
studies.summary_table_title: Four knobs, two readouts, and what each costs at ambient

figures.alt: Three stacked time series over three years of an ambient seasonal cycle: sea temperature oscillating below a dashed maximum-monthly-mean line, the symbiont-to-host ratio settling to a steady value well above a dashed bleaching-criterion line, and the ROS factor sitting steadily above one.
figures.caption: Simulation, control arm. The ambient seasonal cycle with no anomaly, which has to hold before any sweep is read. All seven pre-declared checks pass, including that an unperturbed year accumulates exactly zero degree heating weeks. The footnote records the port check against the published R code.

figures.alt: A three-row, four-column grid, one column per design knob. The top row plots the thermal anomaly at failure on two readouts; the middle row plots the same thresholds in degree heating weeks against shaded NOAA bands, where the host-energy readout sits near zero in three of four panels; the bottom row plots the percentage change in ambient host growth, which is positive for three knobs and negative only for the symbiont thermal optimum.
figures.caption: Simulation, not measurement. The bottom row is the point: raising the symbiont's thermal optimum is the only one of the four knobs that costs anything when there is no heatwave. The middle row shows why the study needed two readouts at all -- degree heating weeks are summed only above a 1 degC HotSpot threshold, so a failure mode that bites below that reads as zero.

figures.alt: Six heatmap panels, one for each pair of the four knobs, each marginalised over the other two, with a shared colour scale for the thermal anomaly at which the host's carbon balance fails.
figures.caption: Simulation. The full four-knob map, marginalised to pairs. Main effects alone explain 0.999 of the variance and all six two-way interactions together add 0.001, so within this box the knobs are additive. That is a property of a four-parameter model, not a claim that two real interventions combine additively in a coral -- which nobody has tested.

studies.title: Branching, plating, massive: a growth-geometry problem, and where the model runs out
studies.kind: accretive growth on a diffusive resource field
studies.question: Colony shape decides flow, light capture, nursery habitat and what a storm breaks. Can a single dimensionless parameter -- the ratio of uptake rate to transport rate that Merks and colleagues identify -- take a colony from massive through to branching? Is the transition sharp or graded, and which metric sees it?
studies.summary: The model class is published and runnable; this implementation is in that family and is not a port of any member of it. Both pre-declared controls pass and the Damkohler sweep moves surface-to-volume, fractal dimension and bounding-box fill smoothly and substantially. The honest result is a failure as well as a finding: the model spans compact mound to open lobed mound and DOES NOT REACH either true branching or plating, so the three-form span this study was built to produce is not achieved. Getting there took three rewrites of the growth rule, and the reason is worth more than the sweep: two earlier voxel versions were dominated by the lattice rather than the physics -- six-connected growth produced octahedra, twenty-six-connected growth produced cubes -- and none of the four declared metrics revealed it. They all varied smoothly and plausibly with the control parameter while the shapes being measured were artefacts. Only looking at the projections showed it.
studies.summary_table_title: What the control parameter moves, and what it does not

figures.alt: A two-row gallery of simulated colonies, side views above and plan views below, running from a smooth compact hemispherical mound at low Damkohler number to progressively rougher and more open lobed mounds at high Damkohler number, with flow-biased and light-weighted variants at the right.
figures.caption: Simulated colonies, one random seed each. These are occupied-voxel silhouettes, not renderings. The gallery is also the evidence for this study's main negative: the high-Damkohler forms are rough open mounds, not separated branches, and no setting tried produced a branching or a plating colony.

figures.alt: A short animation of two simulated colonies growing side by side, side and plan views, one at low Damkohler number staying a smooth compact mound and one at high Damkohler number roughening into an open lobed form, with generation count and voxel volume shown.
figures.caption: Simulated accretive growth, 65 generations at twelve frames a second. Occupied-voxel silhouettes, not renderings; no coral was filmed. The two arms are the ends of the control parameter, so the comparison is the point rather than the motion — and the right-hand arm is also the clearest view of this study's negative, since what it grows into is a rough mound rather than a branching colony.

figures.alt: Four panels against a logarithmic Damkohler axis: branch count, surface-to-volume ratio, box-counting dimension and the area-diameter exponent, each with a shaded band of plus and minus one standard deviation across random seeds, and with the measured exponent ranges for real branching and massive colonies shaded on the last panel.
figures.caption: Simulation. The band is the spread across independent random seeds, not a confidence interval. Only the rightmost panel can be compared with a measurement: the area-diameter exponent is dimensionless, and Chandler and colleagues measured it on real colonies by photogrammetry. The transition verdict uses a cut declared before the sweep was run.

studies.title: The bottleneck nobody engineers: which intervention actually moves surviving recruits
studies.kind: Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis over stated unknowns
studies.question: Restoration does not usually fail because adult corals die. It fails at recruitment. Given larval supply, a settlement cue, and early post-settlement mortality, which intervention moves the most surviving recruits per unit of effort?
studies.summary: This is deliberately a sensitivity analysis and not a point prediction, because the parameters for a prediction do not exist: there is no published value for eggs per colony, wild pelagic larval mortality, no-cue settlement probability, settlers per larva released in the field, or the size at which a recruit escapes incidental grazing. The baseline therefore spans four orders of magnitude, and that is the honest answer rather than a defect. Its own weakness is the cost model: the interventions are ranked per unit of effort and the effort units are mostly invented, with exactly one cost ratio carrying direct published support. The most useful output is not the ranking but the sensitivity decomposition, which shows that about four fifths of the spread comes from stages whose range this page had to invent -- so the highest-value next experiment in this whole chain is a measurement, not a trial.
studies.summary_table_title: Interventions ranked by gain per unit of effort

figures.alt: A horizontal bar chart of each life-history stage's share of the spread in the final recruit count, coloured by whether that stage's range is sourced or assumed, beside a logarithmic percentile strip showing the baseline spanning four orders of magnitude.
figures.caption: Simulation over stated unknowns, not a prediction of any reef. The red bars are stages whose range this page invented because no published value was found, and they dominate. The strip at the right is the point of the whole study: the baseline is a distribution four orders of magnitude wide, and anyone quoting a single number for it is quoting a choice.

figures.alt: Two panels: at the left, each intervention's median multiplier on surviving one-year recruits with a 5th-to-95th-percentile bar on a logarithmic axis; at the right, the same interventions ranked by median gain per unit of relative effort.
figures.caption: Simulation. The left panel's multipliers come from measured effect sizes where those exist; the right panel's ranking additionally depends on effort units that are mostly assumed, which is stated on the figure because it is the weakest link in the comparison. Mass larval enrichment moves the outcome most in absolute terms and site screening wins per unit of effort, and the gap between those two statements is the whole argument about how to spend a restoration budget.
